#4389. 10 Pokémon You Could Take in a Fight

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Have you ever thought about the various types of Pokémon out there? There are some that are quite terrifying. After all, some of them are sharks, others are literal dragons, and there are even Pokémon gods.

Living in the world of Pokémon, you need to be able to defend yourself, and instead of using another Pokémon to fight your battles, you need to start throwing hands. So, I pose the question, “What Pokémon do you think you could take in a fist fight?”

Do you think you are able to beat up an Eevee? Maybe you could take down an Arcanine. Here are some Pokémon you would definitely stand a chance against.

Hear me out, but I think we could all easily take a Ditto in a fight. It has the ability Transform, but in battle, it only transforms into what it is currently fighting. Therefore, the Ditto would transform into you.

Do you think you could take yourself in a fight? I certainly think I could take myself in a fight. It wouldn’t be the easiest battle, but it is certainly better than dealing with a fox that can breathe fire or a mouse that can electrocute you.

You know your strengths and weaknesses, and so all you really need to do is use that to your advantage. Ditto doesn’t know anything about your weaknesses, so you have an advantage.

If it wasn’t obvious, Komala is based on the Koala Bear, and its Pokédex entries make it out to be one in the same. It eats poison leaves that only it can digest. This makes it tired, and it continuously sleeps.

It is said that Komala is asleep from the time it is born to when it dies, and that all of its movements are based on dreams that it is having. This makes it a prime target, and a Pokémon that you could easily take in a fight.

The only issue you may have while fighting this Pokémon is that it will thrash about wildly if you remove the log it is holding. Just don’t mess with its log and you will be fine. It will just think the fight was a dream.

Spoink is an adorable little Pokémon that nobody would ever hurt, but if it came at you looking to fight, you could easily take it. Its Pokédex reveals your entire plan of action, as it states that it needs to keep bouncing in order for its heart to keep beating.

All you need to do is knock it over. It might give you some trouble with its bouncing, but if you can get ahold of its tail, all you need to do is get its back to the ground and its heart will stop.

That is pretty grim, but you have to remember that it is survival of the fittest out there, and Spoink is one of those Pokémon that can easily be defeated with little prep time and some strong actions.

Pokemon isn't all about types and stats. With the right strategy and a bit of training, any Pokemon can be a force to be reckoned with.

Slowpoke is constantly the butt of the joke when it comes to the Pokémon being slow. Its reaction timing is so poor that you could probably land 20 punches before it even realizes what is going on.

Think about it. In the games, people eat Slowpoke tails. It is so common that there are even restaurants in Lumiose City that sell it for dinner every night.

I can only take that as a sign that Slowpoke is easily defeated and captured. How else would they be able to get so many of those tails? After all, you wouldn’t be able to do the same to a Pokémon like Totodile. It would immediately bite your face off.

Sudowoodo would be a terrifying Pokémon to fight, but its pre-evolution, Bonsly, would be an easy victory. Bonsly isn’t much of a fighter, preferring to rest for hours in arid climates.

Enemies don’t typically attack Bonsly because it exudes moisture from its eyes that look like tears. However, we can see through this deception, and that makes us a difficult foe for this Pokémon.

It is said that Bonsly can easily be defeated if it gets too wet, so all you really need to do is dump a bucket of water on it and it is done for. You just need to have no empathy while dealing with this Pokémon or you won’t be able to finish the job.

Some Pokémon are tiny and have barely any defense mechanisms. One such Pokémon is Caterpie. While it may be a cute bug, it is also a bug that you could easily take in a fight.

The only real issue here is that it has a defense mechanism that allows it to release a horrifically foul odor from its body, but if you bring some nose plugs, you will be perfectly fine. Maybe fight it while wearing a gas mask just to be safe.

Other than that, you don’t have to worry about anything from this Pokémon. It has a massive appetite for leaves, so all you really need to do is wait for it to start eating and jump it. Everything will be fine unless you are afraid of them like Misty is.

Milcery is a strange Pokémon, as its body is literally cream. Its Pokédex entry says that it is born from “sweet-smelling particles.” These particles condense into a cream that forms Milcery’s body.

Well, if Milcery is made of cream, that means you just need to eat your way to victory. That sounds like a simple victory to me.

The Pokédex entries give an idea about how this Pokémon fights. It says that Milcery just covers attackers in cream and runs away. In other words, find a way not to get blinded by cream, and you will have no problem taking this Pokémon out. You will even have desert for later.

This list covers the worst Pokémon from generations 1 through 9, and why they fail to capture the attention of players.

Fidough is adorable, there is no denying that one, but it also wouldn’t be difficult to take it in a fight. All it is known for, according to the Pokédex, is producing yeast with its breath to help baked goods rise.

It is also dependent on humans. One of the Pokédex entries says that it has been protected by humans for generations, so it probably doesn’t know how to defend itself without the help of a human companion.

Plus, its short and stubby legs are a bit of a disadvantage. This is a fight that you could easily win. Now, it might be a completely different conversation when Dachsbun is involved, but luckily, we are just talking about Fidough here.

You might see me calling Magikarp weak and pathetic and think that I am just being cruel, but believe me, I am only following what the Pokédex says. Some of the early Pokédex entries say that Magikarp is a weak and pathetic Pokémon that only flops about.

Magikarp is known for getting easily pushed around. It may have some tough scales, but all you need to do is bring a slightly strong weapon and you are golden. Maybe a few kicks would be enough.

During the fight, it will only splash about. Just watch for when it hits seven feet in the air, because that is the height limit for it. You may think the water would save it, but there are so many of them, you are bound to catch one easily.

There are some very weak Pokémon in the games and anime. For instance, Wishiwashi is very weak in its solo form, but I don’t feel like fishing for hours or jumping into the water. However, Sunkern doesn’t have that issue and it is also one of the weakest Pokémon in the game.

With 30 points in each stat and a base stat total of 180, it is amazing that Sunkern can even survive a single battle against any Pokémon. To further show how weak it is, its Pokédex entry says that it tries to move as little as possible to conserve energy.

With how little Sunkern likes to move and how weak it is, I bet anyone could take it in a fight. I’d be shocked if anyone lost to this Pokémon.

From Ultra Necrozma’s stat boosts to Volo’s grueling final battle, these Pokémon encounters bend the rules to deliver memorable challenges.

#4388. Nissan Brings Back the Patrol Name on the 2027 Armada Pro-4X

For the first time since 1969, Nissan will sell a vehicle with the Patrol name in the United States, adding the iconic moniker to the Armada Pro-4X.

There’s a small but significant change coming to the Nissan Armada for 2027. Since the second-generation launched in 2017, the full-size SUV has essentially been a rebadged version of the Patrol SUV sold overseas. Now, the Patrol nameplate will no longer be forbidden fruit. For the 2027 model year, the Armada’s off-road trim has officially been renamed the Armada Patrol Pro-4X.

This is the first time the Patrol nameplate has appeared stateside since 1969, when the second-generation Patrol was offered via Datsun dealerships as the first Nissan-badged vehicle in the U.S. The move to bring back the Patrol name in the U.S. aligns with the off-roader’s 75th anniversary, with production first kicking off in 1951.

See all results for new 2027 Nissan Armada for sale near 53186

The newly renamed model wears a Patrol badge across the rear end, while Armada is printed on the D-pillar. Inside, there are badges that say “Patrol” and “Since 1951” on the center console. The Armada Patrol Pro-4X also adds some new optional equipment, including new NISMO rock sliders and a NISMO roof rack. There are also new NISMO Axis wheels wrapped in BFGoodrich all-terrain tires available for 2027.

Otherwise, the Pro-4X carries over unchanged, still packing an electronic locking rear differential, adaptive air suspension, and a metal underbody skid plate. Under the hood, the twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V-6 remains, still putting out 425 horsepower to all four wheels.

Production of the renamed Armada Patrol Pro-4X begins in November and will be shown for the first time at the 2026 Los Angeles auto show later this month. The Armada Patrol Pro-4X will start at $81,265, a significant increase from last year when it cost $76,575.

#4387. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4386. The Sims 4 gets a bunch of free items inspired by Coach that you can use right now

As part of a free update, The Sims 4 has kicked off a new collaboration with Coach, which means there's free stuff for everyone.

The Sims 4’s first update of the year is here, though it may not be quite what you might have expected. The game’s latest patch mainly centres around a collaboration with Coach, the luxury fashion brand.

This obviously isn’t the game’s first collaboration with a known brand, though this one does include a lot of free items and accessories that anyone can make use of, even if they don’t care about Coach.

The Coach Collection brings nine new items to The Sims 4. They range from clothes and accessories you can use with Create a Sim, to decoration items available in Build Buy. There’s also The Carriage House, a new Gallery household where you can find three new roommates.

There’s a nice bit of variety in the options available, some casual and others more practical for your Sims to wear. Then there’s The Bag Room, which can also be grabbed from the Gallery. The room simply serves as a way for you to show off your Coach bags and trunks collection.

In case you missed it, The Sims’ development team recently shared an update on some of what we can expect in 2026, both for The Sims 4 as well as other projects currently in the works. It even included further confirmation, if any was needed, that Project Rene is a dedicated mobile off-shoot, and not — as many had long believed — The Sims 5.

The blog post also included a statement about EA’s imminent change of ownership, which many fear could alter the series’ inclusive and diverse nature, and the decisions made by its various teams.

#4384. Subcompact SUVs May Seem Appealing, but Compact Cars Are Often a Better Buy

Unless you’re dead-set on the tall seating position that an SUV provides, we think these small hatchbacks are far more satisfying than their crossover siblings.

Sure, SUVs are popular, but that doesn’t mean they’re always the best choice for your needs. The smaller an SUV gets, the fewer advantages it offers when compared with an equivalent sedan or hatchback. Here, we’re looking at the subcompact SUV segment and stacking up these small crossovers against compact cars from the same brand.

Subcompact SUVs are the smallest of their species. As the name suggests, they’re smaller than compact SUVs, and their tidier footprints often mean compromises in space, fuel economy, and driving satisfaction.

Automakers feel the need to offer additional ground clearance and all-wheel drive in these SUV models to justify their categorization. But these models typically share the same underpinnings and engines as their compact-car kin.

This means these SUV models are often heavier, less enjoyable to drive, and less fuel-efficient than their non-SUV siblings. Both types of vehicles also typically offer similar amounts of cargo and passenger space. Pricing, meanwhile, tends to favor the compact hatchbacks.

If these two types of vehicles are so similar, then why the different classifications? Blame size creep.

Cars and SUVs typically get larger with each passing generation. Let’s roll the clock back 25 years. While most modern compact cars are bigger than their counterparts from a quarter century ago, they still tend to cast smaller shadows than mid-size cars from the turn of the millennium.

On the other hand, the subcompact SUVs of today are typically larger than the compact SUVs of 25 years ago. Due to this, calling a modern SUV “subcompact” better describes its size relative to the overall SUV landscape as opposed to the larger passenger-vehicle space.

Odds are that if you’re shopping for one of these small-sized SUVs, you’re going to be just as well—if not better—served by these vehicles’ often less expensive and more fun-to-drive compact hatchback stablemates.

The HR-V is Honda's smallest SUV, but it’s still plenty spacious inside. The main downside of this model is that it’s available with only one powertrain: a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter inline-four that produces just 158 horsepower.

This means the HR-V accelerates at a leisurely pace. In our testing, this little Honda SUV needed 9.4 seconds to hit 60 mph.

The HR-V earns an EPA-estimated combined rating of 28 mpg in front-drive form. Adding all-wheel drive drops that figure to 27 mpg.

The Honda Civic hatchback has the same base engine as the CR-V, but it also offers a more powerful and more fuel-efficient hybrid variant that has quicker acceleration and much better fuel economy—up to 49 mpg combined, according to the EPA. The Civic doesn’t offer all-wheel drive as the HR-V does, but we’d advocate for a good set of winter tires instead.

In our testing, the Civic hatchback’s cargo area was only marginally smaller than the HR-V’s. It held six carry-on suitcases behind the rear seat, which is only one fewer case than the HR-V can accommodate.

More importantly, the Civic is far more fun to drive than the HR-V.

A redesign for 2027 brings eye-catching new looks to the Kia Seltos subcompact SUV. A 147-hp four-cylinder comes standard, while a 190-hp turbo four is optional. For its second generation, the Seltos also offers an available gas-electric hybrid powertrain—an option the Kia K4 compact hatch lacks.

Sure, the Kia K4 hatchback doesn’t offer hybrid power. However, what this handsome hatch lacks in powertrain options, it makes up for in other ways.

Simply put, we prefer the way the K4 drives to the Seltos. Credit the compact hatchback’s lower center of gravity, which improves handling and behind-the-wheel engagement.

The K4 is also more miserly than the equivalent gas-only Seltos. When fitted with the available 190-hp turbocharged 1.6-liter four-cylinder, the K4 hatch is also notably quicker than its equally powerful Seltos kin. In our testing, a so-equipped K4 hatch accelerated to 60 mph in 7.0 seconds, while a turbocharged Seltos needed 8.2 seconds to hit the same mark.

We haven’t yet measured how many carry-on suitcases fit in the cargo bay of the new Seltos. Compared to the previous-generation Seltos, though, the K4 hatch fell one carry-on suitcase short of its subcompact SUV sibling’s sum.

The Subaru Crosstrek is the spiritual successor to the old Impreza Outback Sport, which was essentially an Impreza hatchback with added body cladding. Compared to the old Outback Sport, the Crosstrek is a bit more distinct than the Impreza it’s based on. Even so, the Crosstrek is still effectively a lifted Impreza hatch with additional ground clearance and more rugged looks. As such, we don’t think the Crosstrek is worth the extra cost over the run-of-the-mill Impreza hatchback that Subaru still offers.

Subaru makes an even better case for the Impreza hatch for 2027 courtesy of a new base model that starts at less than $26,000. As we previously detailed, the Impreza beats the Crosstrek in nearly every metric in our testing: It’s quicker, more fuel-efficient, and offers as much space inside. The only reason we can think of to choose the Crosstrek is for its available gas-electric hybrid powertrain or its extra ground clearance.

The Mazda CX-30 is among our favorite subcompact crossover SUVs. It drives great, features a high-quality interior, and provides sufficient oomph with the standard 186-hp 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine. Opt for the 250-hp turbocharged 2.5-liter, and the all-wheel-drive CX-30 accelerates with even more vigor. But what if Mazda also sold a vehicle that paired all the positive traits of the CX-30 with a lower starting price, even better driving dynamics, and an available manual gearbox? Well, good news: It does.

The Mazda 3 hatchback may do without the higher seating position of the CX-30, but it makes up for it with livelier dynamics courtesy of its lower center of gravity and lighter curb weight. At a manufacturer-estimated 3111 pounds, the front-drive 3 hatch’s mass undercuts that of the all-wheel-drive CX-30 by 284 pounds.

While we think the available six-speed manual gearbox of the front-drive 3 makes it superior to its all-wheel-drive kin, we know not everyone will agree with us. No worries, though, because Mazda also offers the 3 with all-wheel drive. Opting for it adds 172 pounds to the curb weight of 3 hatchbacks with the standard 186-hp four. However, AWD is standard on turbocharged models.

In our testing, both the 3 hatchback and CX-30 were able to hold up to 16 carry-on suitcases with the rear seats folded. With the rear seats in place, the 3 hatch’s cargo area held five carry-on suitcases—just one fewer than the CX-30.

Acura’s subcompact SUV is about as interesting and exciting as watching C-SPAN. Short of its available all-wheel-drive system and slightly bigger interior compartment, there are few other reasons to pick the ADX over its compact hatchback sibling, the Integra.

With a starting price of $34,795, the Acura Integra undercuts the ADX by a significant $1755. It’s also significantly more enjoyable to drive and a good deal quicker.

Though both the Integra and ADX come standard with a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine that mates to a continuously variable automatic transmission (CVT), the Integra benefits from an extra 10 horsepower and 13 pound-feet of torque relative to the unit in the ADX. With 200 horsepower and 192 pound-feet of torque, a CVT-equipped Integra accelerated to 60 mph in a reasonable 7.1 seconds. An all-wheel-drive ADX, meanwhile, required a languid 8.7 ticks to hit 60 mph.

Admittedly, the fastback shape of the Integra cuts into its cargo-carrying capabilities. We fit 18 carry-on suitcases in its cargo bay with the rear seats folded and five with the seatbacks up. The squarer shape of the ADX afforded totals of 22 and seven, respectively.

Despite being raised on a steady diet of base-model Hondas and Toyotas—or perhaps because of it—Joey Capparella cultivated an obsession for the automotive industry throughout his childhood in Nashville, Tennessee. He found a way to write about cars for the school newspaper during his college years at Rice University, which eventually led him to move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, for his first professional auto-writing gig at Automobile Magazine. He has been part of the Hearst Autos team since 2016 and now lives in New York City.

Despite their shared last name, Greg Fink is not related to Ed "Big Daddy" Roth's infamous Rat Fink. Both Finks, however, are known for their love of cars, car culture, and—strangely—monogrammed one-piece bathing suits. Greg's career in the media industry goes back more than a decade. His previous experience includes stints as an editor at publications such as U.S. News & World Report, The Huffington Post, Motor1.com, and MotorTrend.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several new customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

#4379. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4378. 7 Video Games That Could Sweep in The Game Awards, Ranked

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Winter holidays bring joy through family gatherings and discounted video games, but they have also become synonymous with awards ceremonies celebrating the year's finest releases.

In the case at hand, 2026 has established itself as a magnificent trip around the sun thanks to the numerous masterful titles that have been, or will be, released during its 12 months, making for a fiercely contested race to see which is the best.

The number of events held for this purpose is as vast as it is diverse, although all eyes are on December 10th, the day the interactive industry's Ballon d'Or is awarded.

Therefore, if you're as eager as I am to see if any video game can come close to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's phenomenal success last year, I recommend you read this list of seven video games that could sweep The Game Awards, ranked.

The first and most underrated video game to appear on this list is none other than Big Walk, a game that will arrive completely silent despite having the power to surprise more than a few on this special night.

That it will win Best Multiplayer should be a given, but this would be merely the bare minimum of the recognition that House House's team has earned through one of the most special and creative indie games of recent years.

Because of this, and considering it's this year's highest-rated game on Metacritic if we don't count remasters and remakes, there's more than enough reason to believe it could become 2026's most acclaimed independent production.

My bets for Game Direction and Audio Design are bolder, especially since these are usually awarded to larger projects with bigger budgets. However, given what happened last year, I wouldn't rule out Big Walk silencing more than a few detractors.

This article ranks the Game of the Year nominee classes from The Game Awards each year of the 2020s.

A particularly curious case is that of Control Resonant, which presents itself as a solid piece in numerous departments, even though I don't believe its overall acclaim is sufficient to be a Game of the Year contender.

Said detail aside, Remedy knows what it's like to have a string of successes after Alan Wake 2 won three of its eight nominations in 2023, and its latest project could repeat that feat with even greater force.

Specifically, in terms of the audiovisual component, it's by far one of the year's strongest contenders, which hasn't stood out for its narratives or art direction at Control Resonant's level, except in the indie scene.

That a title can win so many awards without being Game of the Year already happened in 2022 with God of War: Ragnarök, and for reasons very similar to those experienced by Kratos's latest adventure, I think we could be facing the same scenario now.

Capcom has been, arguably by a wide margin, the most outstanding developer of the year, having released Monster Hunter Stories 3, Pragmata, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, and, most relevantly for this occasion, Resident Evil: Requiem.

Angela Sant'Albano's stellar performance as Grace Ashcroft already guarantees a strong chance of winning an award despite the fierce competition, as does its status as the best horror game of the year and all that entails in terms of gameplay and audio design.

From there, Resident Evil: Requiem faces an uphill battle to win all the awards for which it will surely be a candidate, as it is undeniably one of the best games of the year.

Will being the best Resident Evil be enough to secure every possible nomination? Time will tell, but its candidacy and the seriousness with which it must be approached can be anticipated from this very moment.

The Game Awards has six awesome titles up for Game Of The Year in 2025, but here are seven more that still feel like they've been snubbed.

The Game Awards' biggest winners last year ranged from indie to AA titles, opening up a world of possibilities for this and future iterations, especially for extraordinary adventures like Mina the Hollower.

The current lineup isn't as fertile for indie products to take center stage as it did in 2025, but I'm certain that, if any prospect can truly achieve that, it's Yacht Club Games' masterpiece.

As for Best Indie Game, Best Action-Adventure Game, and Game Direction, I'd bet my life that this wonderful ode to classic video games will be in the running, aiming to take home those awards, though it's outstanding enough in the other categories to warrant consideration as well.

The interactive medium's pendulum is increasingly swinging in favor of indie games in these turbulent times, where the biggest companies keep making bad decisions, so Mina the Hollower could capitalize on those protest votes.

The year's not-so-surprise surprise is Phantom Blade Zero, which stands on the shoulders of Black Myth: Wukong to likely become the Chinese video game with the most nominations and prizes at The Game Awards.

As part of the top three contenders for the People's Choice Award, I see S-Game's gem as a work robust enough to compete with the two titans that you and I both know round out this list, which says everything you need to know about its quality.

Its greatest strength is its unique character, stemming from a singular design, composition, and presentation philosophy that we've seen only a handful of times, allowing it to stand out with literally unparalleled ease and fluidity among the rest.

It has more than enough quality to win any title it's given, so much so that, if we were in any other year of the decade, I could easily predict that Phantom Blade Zero would be GOTY.

The Best Games For Impact Nominees Of All Time are emotional and thought-provoking experiences.

Nevertheless, the year is 2026, and it just so happens that it coincides with the return of what many consider the best video game of all time, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake.

If there's one reason why I feel most action-adventure games will have a tough time, it's because the quintessential adventure has returned, the one that paved the way for the entire genre in the three decades following its release.

From the music to its underrated art direction, including its technical and gameplay splendor, it's safe to say that the Ocarina of Time remake will be present even in the Muppet segments created by the legendary Geoff Keighley.

In 1998, there was no The Game Awards to give Link's odyssey the recognition it deserved, so don't be surprised if the video game industry, as a whole, makes this year the perfect moment to rectify that omission.

If we take into account what its immediate predecessor did and what its creators have promised to do with it, there's no doubt that the top contender to sweep The Game Awards is Grand Theft Auto 6.

Rockstar is fully aware that, every year they release a game, December becomes a month of metaphorical and material praise, given their habit of releasing the most ambitious and massive titles the industry is ready to see.

Link is a formidable competitor, and that's indisputable, yet Lucia and Jason have the added momentum of being the most anticipated video game in history and the most expensive ever made, making them immediate candidates for a third of the event's categories.

It's difficult to predict with certainty, though if there's one thing I can be partially sure of, it's that Ocarina of Time and GTA 6 will quickly make this article obsolete by taking home practically every award between them.

These titles were left at the gates of glory, but they deserved to be called Game of the Year.

#4376. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

#4375. The best soft launch mobile games for iPhone, iPad or Android

The biggest games yet to launch on the global market

If you've been looking for something new and exciting that isn't quite fully released, then look no further; you've found our list of the best games currently in soft launch.

Sometimes developers like to make sure the paying public is willing to play their game before they push it to every device in the world - that's where soft launch comes in. Available in just a handful of countries and regions, a soft-launched game is subject to drastic change as developers take on board customer feedback (and other metrics) to alter the game and ensure the best possible product is ready for when it goes to worldwide launch.

But here's the kicker - we can see when developers do that. And when you're looking at some of the big games, like the ones we have on this list, then you can find yourself getting very excited, and even a little jealous that you can't play them yet.

So to help you out a little, we've collected a huge list of some of the biggest and best games currently available in soft launch, which you might well be able to get if you have the right Apple ID or Google Play account to download them with.

Just as a note: In the case of a game suddenly disappearing, it might be because the developer has decided to stop development on it early and save themselves the cost of a big launch, or because the developer is gearing up for a big launch and wants to surprise the world. Whatever the case, we'll try to keep you updated when these things happen.

Let's get into the list! SoulTerra Odyssey

An interesting one here. Bandai Namco has dived back into the mobile world with a completely new IP. They're also claiming it's the first 'Match3D Roguelite Battle Game ever.' Given the sheer breadth of games out there, I highly doubt it, but it's an intriguing combination, nonetheless.

Sonic Rumble sees the blue blur returning to mobile, this time as a battle royale of sorts. In the mould of games like Stumble Guys and Fall Guys, it appears we can expect to dash around obstacle-filled courses, dodging the numerous hazards that threaten to eliminate us at every turn. It's definitely a setup that suits Sonic and co, but is it entering a market that's already been conquered by Scopely? Only time will tell.

Casual strategy games are all the rage these days, particularly on mobile. Anything that gives you a slight hit of feeling clever without requiring in-depth tactics that take forever to learn. Century Games' Crown of Bones is the latest attempt at sliding into that niche. It sees you joining the Skeleton King and his army as they battle through numerous realms. It sports a colourful art style that reminds me somewhat of little toy towns and villages, something you might have created in real life as a child, perhaps. As for the gameplay, it pretty much consists of increasing your numbers, upgrading your troops and toppling your opponents. There are a few special items thrown in for good measure as well.

If you're a football fan, you're probably already aware of Nordeus as the folks behind the popular management sim Top Eleven. With their latest effort, Top Goal, they are swapping the touchline for the pitch as you take direct control over your squad, having a more active role in the outcome of a match. Still, it seems some of the strategic side remains as you build your squad and choose your formation before taking on other players in PvP.

While it might seem as though the era of endless runners has passed on mobile, several still do very well, particularly if they have brand power behind them. Zapak hopes that Ben 10 Alien Run can join that list, putting a lot of stock in the popular children's cartoon pulling in the younger generation.

In it, you will dash around while transforming into one of nine different aliens, each bringing special abilities to the table. That might be creating a shield to block an enemy attack in one instance, while another might clear the path ahead with laser beams. On top of that, there are the usual daily challenges and missions you'd expect from the genre.

Oh My Anne is a match-3 game based on the popular novel series Anne of Green Gables. Players proceed through the story by completing levels and associated challenges. It's certainly interesting to see Neowiz deciding to take established, historical (1908~) novels and their IP and spin them off into games. There's a question to be asked about brand recognition and 'crossover IP' when those IPs are not ones from the current vogue. We regularly see Warhammer and Marvel crossover games, but those things are currently 'in', Anne of Green Gables — and Oh My Anne — targets a different audience and plays by different rules of advertising. Could there be a Dracula, Canterbury Tales or Beowulf games on the horizon if this takes off?

NetEase's Stumble Guys killer, Eggy Party, is rapidly moving toward its global release with seven new regions granted access to it in January of 2024; before that, it was simply in the SEA region. What's the big appeal? Well, if you're not sold by the constant party, cheerful colours and multiplayer mania of Eggy Party, then maybe the map creation will be the thing to grab your attention. A bumbling race to the finish might be fun, but doing it on a map that you - or one of your friends - created is vastly more fun.

Zynga, who you likely know for, well, many things, are working on a new addition to their growing merge catalogue. FruitFall – don't forget the double capital Fs – tasks you with merging fruits to beat each level. Simple, right? Judging by the store description, expect this to become more difficult as you progress. At first, it'll likely be a case of simply merging fruit, while the latter stages will introduce troublesome crates and frozen fruit that need thawing out before becoming useful. Zynga claims each level brings something different, keeping the challenge fresh and fun. Time will tell if that's the case

Mattel Match: Toybox looks to bring together the company's many toys under one roof, including Uno, Masters of the Universe and, of course, Barbie. How? You might ask. Through match-3 puzzling, that's how.

As you'll likely have guessed from the name, Puzzletown Mysteries sees you unravel mysteries by solving puzzles. There is also a town involved. The overarching whodunit is whether poor Gladys slipped from her balcony or if she received a little push before toppling over the edge, while you'll also look into a case of stolen cats.

As you've likely already guessed from the name, we're talking tower defence here. Here, the slight twist on the usual formula is that, alongside setting up your various defences, you'll actually build the map your enemies will march down. Of course, that's something we've seen before, but it's a fun twist nevertheless. I'm quite fond of the visuals, which have a super clean and easy-to-read look that's just shy of qualifying as minimalist.

Diamond Dreams is looking to bring a sense of elegance to the match-3 genre. The whole idea is that you're working towards crafting some stunning jewellery that, I have to say, looks far better than it possibly needs to.

Given the immense popularity of Monopoly Go, it seemed inevitable that similar games would pop up eventually. Coin Master – Board Adventure from Moon Active is one such attempt. Having already achieved success with Coin Master, I'd imagine this will also do incredibly well.

Cats & Soup has made a name for itself in recent times with its lovely aesthetic and focus on feline companions. While it's still a fairly familiar idle RPG, the focus on cosiness helped it stand out from a massive crowd. Evidently buoyed by its success, a spin-off called Cats & Soup: Magic Recipe is now in the works. Once again, the team are taking on a familiar mobile genre, bringing some warm-fuzzy cuteness to the merge-and-match realm. The aim is to cook delicious recipes, build a lovely home for your kitties, and make friends with new cats.

The humble match-3 will likely never lose popularity on mobile. It's simple to understand and great for playing on the go since it hits a nice spot between relaxing and engaging the brain. It's not surprising, then, that we often have big franchises delve into the genre. The latest to try their white-gloved hand is Disney with Disney Magic Match 3D. In it, you'll remove colourful clutter. No, really. Check out Catherine's preview to learn more.

While George R R Martin might have no interest in finishing his own book series, there is still plenty of Game of Thrones content to enjoy. Dragonfire is the latest, a tile-based strategy game that lets you put the titular fire-breathing winged beasties to work. But it's not simply sending them into battle. You will hatch and train them, taking your little fiery friend from a cute baby to a creature capable of barbecuing enemy villages.

We all love Fruit Ninja, but if there's one criticism you can throw its way, it's that it didn't have much else going for it beyond slicing up fruit. Adventure looks to change this by introducing a level-based approach that sees you solving puzzles alongside stabbing melons. You can also unlock new weapons and abilities as you progress, presumably allowing you to dice a kiwi in untold ways.

FairyTale Quest is a roguelite action RPG in the style of something like Vampire Survivors. And its characters? Well, as you've likely guessed, they're all pulled from traditional stories. So you can expect the Big Bad Wolf and Red Riding Hood to fight by your side. They can put aside their differences for the greater good, it seems.

That's right. Plants Vs Zombies 3 is back in soft launch, this time with Evolved after the colon. This refers to the merging mechanics they're throwing in with their latest attempt. We'll see how that all pans out in due course, but it's hard not to be a little sceptical given that EA has clearly struggled to figure out what they want to do with PvZ.

It's been almost ten years since Hill Climb Racing 2 launched, so it likely feels about time for a sequel for fans of wacky, physics-based driving. In the third instalment, you can expect plenty of special gadgets and handy boosts for increasing your performance on the bouncy track. There are also the plentiful customisation options on offer that any self-respecting racer needs. If we can't pimp our ride, what's the point?

Aside from the obvious flock and little green candy-loving monster, there are few games more iconic on mobile than Temple Run. That's why the announcement of a third has got us excited here at Pocket Gamer. But do those simple yet effective mechanics stand up after all these years, or are massive changes needed? Well, check out Catherine's Temple Run 3 preview to see what she thought.

Cute little penguins running around an obstacle course in Fall/Stumble Guys fashion? Haven't we already seen this with Pudgy Party? Apparently, Smilegate thinks they can do better, and personally, I'm all for it. Penguins are wonderful little creatures, and the more games where they're the star, the better. It sees you participating in 10-minute matches where the aim is to get your beak across the line first.

If you love pinging marbles and cutesy creatures, Marblebound might be the perfect fit for you. You gather a team of four heroes and then head into battle to take down a series of fearsome foes. And you'll do that by firing marbles at them, including ricocheting them off walls if you know your angles.

FunPlus, who you may know from State of Survival and DC: Dark Legion, among others, appears to be working on a new game. This one's called Dark Shot Survival and sees you building up a base to fend off night creatures (yes, they look like zombies to me, too). The whole thing seems to centre around a day/night cycle, wherein you spend the waking hours gathering resources and fortifying your base. Then, when the sun goes down, you'll need to fend off the zomb— sorry, night creatures, with all your might.

Angry Birds Rush sees Rovio's recognisable avians slinging themselves into a different genre. By the looks of things, Rush is an endless runner that sees you bouncing through various colourful locales all inspired by the series' many other games. It doesn't appear to be a straightforward runner, though, with slingshot elements still present to some extent.

There are few cartoon duos more iconic than Tom & Jerry. I'm not even a huge fan of them, but they'd certainly spring to mind if I had to name two long-standing cartoon rivals. It's that instant recognition that probably helped Steer Studios decide it was an IP worth working with. Tom and Jerry Blast is a puzzler that, based on the screenshots, sees you tapping your way through each level and using boosters if they ever become overly tricky.

You wouldn't necessarily put sailing the seven seas and tower defence together, but that's exactly what Puzala is going for with Stormborn Era. In it, you take charge of Black Sam and his crew, defending their ship from the hordes of enemies that have nothing better to do with their time than attack a big boat.

The Girls' Frontline series has proven incredibly popular over the years. Apparently, conventionally attractive women with guns will always do well. Who knew? Anyway, you can check out Catherine's Ahead of the Game to see if it's more than just a surface-level shooter.

Having briefly appeared in the US a while back, Borderlands Mobile has crept back into soft launch in Canada. The latest iteration has revealed that we can play as long-time fan-favourite Mad Moxxi, which I'm sure will be welcome news to many folks.
